body:
If I understand correctly, the model you're proposing here is one where the TSM is both the attestation verifier and the key/secret broker. A more generic local attestation model extends that architecture to the verifier being any trustworthy component on the same physical platform, which could be the TSM or e.g. another TVM with which the attester can establish an out of bound secure link. The same applies to the secret broker: Having the TSM playing that role is a sensible architecture, but we could imagine here that it could also be some other entity in the platform (another TVM, the platform RoT, etc).

I think we should allow for supporting a generic local attestation model and not restrict this spec to the specific implementation you're proposing here, where the local verifier and the local secret broker happen to be the same trusted entity: the TSM.

For that purpose, I think we should first describe the generic local attestation flow for `CoVE`, that would look pretty similar to the remote attestation one. The attester requests an attestation evidence from the TSM but instead of sending it to a remote third party, submits it to e.g. another TVM through an implementation specific, trusted interface (e.g. following the [trustee attestation protocol](https://github.com/confidential-containers/trustee/blob/main/kbs/docs/kbs_attestation_protocol.md)). Following this we can describe how a `CoVE` TSM could, as a specific implementation of thee generic local attestation architecture, be used as either a verifier, a secret broker or both, and I think we want to differentiate those two services. This could be a sub section of the generic local attestation one:

- TSM as a local verifier: In that case the TVM could use e.g. an optional `sbi_covt_attest()` SBI function to ask the TSM to attest to it, based on the same material that the attestation token is built upon. Assuming the TSM supports that service and has been provisioned with a set of attestation policies, then the TSM could attest the TVM and returned a signed attestation token. An IETF standard for attestation tokens is [EAR](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-rats-ear-01.html). With an `EAR` attestation token, the TVM can now choose to request a secret, from a local or remote secret broker. The TSM **could** be such broker, in which case the TVM could submit the token to it.
- TSM as a secret broker: Assuming the TSM has also been provisioned with a set of protected and uniquely identified secrets and their related policies (mapping TVM claims to secrets), the TVM could call into the `sbi_covt_get_secret(eat_token, secret_id)` function and attempt to get a secret released from the TSM. The TSM, as a secret broker, would verify and then evaluate the received attestation token against the requested secret policy and decide if the secret can be delivered to the requesting TVM or not.

I understand this is a bit more complex than what the current PR is proposing, but I think it would make the specification generic enough to support a wider set of use cases, including the one you're proposing. I'm definitely ready to help with the next level of details if you think the above changes make sense.

cc @jyao1

+
+
+=== Local Attestation
+
+Systems that cannot rely on remote attestation due to unreliable network
+might use local attestation, in which the TSM attests to the integrity of the
+TVM and conditions under which it executes using the rules defined in a TVM
+attestation payload (TAP), a cryptographically protected file created by the
+authorized entity (TVM creator).
+
+[NOTE]
+====
+The TAP can be provided to the TSM at the time of the TVM creation or runtime.
+In the former case, the TSM can enforce that a TVM is allowed to execute and
+might provide it with a boot key. In the latter, it can provide the TVM with
+continuous access to secrets as part of a licensing model.
+====
+
+Local attestation utilizes one or more of the following properties:
+
+. TVM–Platform Binding: The TSM verifies that a TVM creator authorized the TVM
+to run on the platform.
+. TVM Authorization: The TSM enforces that only TVMs created by a trusted entity
+(e.g., a TVM creator) runs on the hardware.
+
+A CoVE-enabled platform supporting the TVM-platform binding must consist of a
+mechanism to identify the platform, for example via cryptographic keys exposed
+by an implementation-specific mechanism, such as a hardware root of trust with
+support for CoVE DICE.
+The creator of a TVM must then be able to link the identity key with the
+hardware and use it to encode the TAP.
+Only the TSM running on that platform must have access to the key that permits
+it to decode the TAP. Access to such key should be linked to the integrity of
+all TCB elements, such as the TSM and other M-mode firmware.
+After successful local attestation, the TVM should be able to request the TSM to
+retrieve secrets encoded in the TAP using an ABI call
+(`sbi_covg_retrieve_secret()`).
+
+A CoVE-enabled platform supporting the TVM authorization must restrict what
+TVMs are allowed to run. There must be an implementation-specific mechanism to
+provide the TSM with a list of public keys of those authorized to sign TVM
+images for execution on the platform. The creator of a TVM must sign the TAP
+associated with the TVM with the corresponding private key. During local
+attestation, the TSM verifies the signature inside the TAP using the list of
+authorized public keys to decide if the TVM is authorized to execute. If the
+signature is not valid, the TSM rejects to promote the VM to TVM.
+
+[id=tap_format]
+[caption="Figure {counter:image}"]
+[title= ": Format of the TVM Attestation Payload (TAP)"]
+image::tap_format.png[align=center]

Since we do not know the final list of attribute types (might be defined in future specs), then we kept the attribute list confidential. One could imagine a system-specific licencing key that could be encoded as part of the attributes that would have to remain secret. 

When it comes to the measurement section, in some deployments, the VM image might contain encrypted kernel, and keeping the measurements section public would disclose the version of the kernel inside a TVM. Since the measurement section could also define measurements of OS/VMM to enforce specific load time integrity of the hypervisor and the TVM at the same time, one would disclose what enforcement level is required for particular TVM image. Whether the latter is the real problem is arguable. 

Do you have specific use cases where keeping such information public would be helpful, e.g., for resource orchestration, scheduling etc?

> Since we do not know the final list of attribute types (might be defined in future specs), then we kept the attribute list confidential. One could imagine a system-specific licencing key that could be encoded as part of the attributes that would have to remain secret.
> 

I may be misunderstanding how the attributes on the TAP would be verified, but I am assuming it would be compared against anything that the TSM would use to generate the attestation evidence. Do you envision that a licensing key could be added to the TVM attestation evidence at TVM build time? Typically, there are no secrets in such evidence.

> When it comes to the measurement section, in some deployments, the VM image might contain encrypted kernel, and keeping the measurements section public would disclose the version of the kernel inside a TVM.

Sure, but the measurement itself being a crypto hash, would hide this, right? You'd have the TSM comparing measurements of the TVM against TAP measurements, both being crypto hashes.

> Since the measurement section could also define measurements of OS/VMM to enforce specific load time integrity of the hypervisor and the TVM at the same time, one would disclose what enforcement level is required for particular TVM image. Whether the latter is the real problem is arguable.
> 
> Do you have specific use cases where keeping such information public would be helpful, e.g., for resource orchestration, scheduling etc?

For transparency and debugging sake, for example. If your TVM is denied a secret release, you'd want to be able to understand why from the TVM itself. Reciprocally, you may want to understand/verify why you got a secret from a TSM. Attestation tokens you get from remote verifiers are expected to provide that level of transparency.

> I may be misunderstanding how the attributes on the TAP would be verified, but I am assuming it would be compared against anything that the TSM would use to generate the attestation evidence. Do you envision that a licensing key could be added to the TVM attestation evidence at TVM build time? Typically, there are no secrets in such evidence.

Licensing key was an example I made up to demonstrate that there might be attributes in future that require confidentiality. Remember that we do not have a fixed list of attributes that people will use since we do not know all possible use cases that will show up. 

Let's extend this example a bit and imagine three parties: a car manufacturer, an autonomous driving module provider, and a car owner. A car manufacturer wants to limit what companies are allowed to extend car's functionalities with extra features, so he maintains some form of a licensing system. The autonomous driving module provider wants to sell his product to a car owner and run the autonomous driving feature in a TVM to protect his IP. When a car owner buys an autonomous driving module, the provider creates a TAP ensuring that a TVM accesses secrets only when ran on the particular instance of the car. This TAP must also contain a licensing key issued by the car manufacturer to the module provider, otherwise TSM will reject running this feature on the car. Since a car might have limited network connectivity, the TSM must make decision to release secrets to a TVM without network, thus local attestation. In this example, the licensing key would be a secret token that the car manufacturer releases to a module provider. Obviously, there might be other implementations, maybe better ones, based on asymmetric crypto, where a list of public keys of module providers are somehow embedded in a system and the TSM could verify a signature issued by the module provider.

> Sure, but the measurement itself being a crypto hash, would hide this, right? You'd have the TSM comparing measurements of the TVM against TAP measurements, both being crypto hashes.

Regarding the measurement section, yes, a crypto hash will hide the contents of the TVM image. Except for the fact that anyone seeing TAP understands whom it belongs to and what measurements will be verified, I agree that this section could be public, i.e., no confidentiality but only integrity protected. Maybe @gdhh has some more thoughts?

> For transparency and debugging sake, for example. If your TVM is denied a secret release, you'd want to be able to understand why from the TVM itself. Reciprocally, you may want to understand/verify why you got a secret from a TSM. Attestation tokens you get from remote verifiers are expected to provide that level of transparency.

The owner of a TVM should be able to view a TAP in plaintext when he needs. Specifically, he can embed a lockbox that can be decrypted/decapsulated only with his private key to access to the TSK. If the TSM rejects giving a TVM secrets, then the question is rather which measurements and attributes failed verification and this information is not available statically inside a TAP but in runtime. I imagine that a TSM could report an error with an information like "failed to verify measurement register 0" or "licensing_key does not match". If the TVM gets access to secrets, then it means that all conditions from TAP were satisfied and the TVM owner can view these conditions by inspecting a TAP.

> sbi_covt_get_secret(eat_token, secret_id)

I see that the architecture could be extended to a one where secret broker and a verifier could be separated entity. In a specific case in which a TSM would wear both of these hats, a token would be just extra unnecessary piece of information because a TSM knows the requester's identity, i.e., what TVM requests a secrets. Thus, the TSM will only look for secrets associated with this particular TVM, right? Or there are use cases in which one TVM could requests secrets of another TVM when these TVMs exchange (or steal) tokens?

> For that purpose, I think we should first describe the generic local attestation flow for CoVE, that would look pretty similar to the remote attestation one. The attester requests an attestation evidence from the TSM but instead of sending it to a remote third party, submits it to e.g. another TVM through an implementation specific, trusted interface (e.g. following the [trustee attestation protocol](https://github.com/confidential-containers/trustee/blob/main/kbs/docs/kbs_attestation_protocol.md)). Following this we can describe how a CoVE TSM could, as a specific implementation of thee generic local attestation architecture, be used as either a verifier, a secret broker or both, and I think we want to differentiate those two services. This could be a sub section of the generic local attestation one:

I see the flow for releasing a token and using a token to retrieve secrets. What I am missing is how a TVM, which acts as a local secret broker, provisions the secrets in scenarios where only local attestation (no network) is available? It needs some component in the TCB, like the TSM or maybe RoT, to provide it with at least a key to decrypt other TVMs' TAPs. If this job is done by a TSM then we end up with the currently proposed model. If a TVM has access to a RoT, then this TVM becomes somehow special, more privileged "architectural" TVM. We would need to ensure at the architecture level that only this TVM can access the key in RoT.

Other question is how other TVMs will retrieve the secrets? If the communicate with a TSM via `sbi_covt_get_secret()` then a TSM must somehow access the secret inside a local secret broker, right? Or would `sbi_covt_get_secret()` be somehow routed TVM->TSM->OS/VMM->TSM->LocalSecretBroker->TSM->OS/VMM->TSM->TVM?

body:
> > sbi_covt_get_secret(eat_token, secret_id)
> 
> I see that the architecture could be extended to a one where secret broker and a verifier could be separated entity. In a specific case in which a TSM would wear both of these hats, a token would be just extra unnecessary piece of information because a TSM knows the requester's identity, i.e., what TVM requests a secrets.
>

I agree, yes. However skipping this step means you'd have an optional argument to the attest SBI function for cases where you'd want to get a secret from the TSM while attesting, making the SBI more cumbersome. IMHO the API complexity cost of an additional, optional argument is higher than one additional call to pass the token back to the TSM. Having separated APIs for verification vs secret delivery makes for a clearer separation of duties between those two services.

> Thus, the TSM will only look for secrets associated with this particular TVM, right?
>

You want to associate secrets to a particular set of attested claims, not necessarily a specific TVM. That's a secret policy definition. In other words, two exact same TVMs could get the same secret from the TSM because they'd have the exact same attestation token.

> Or there are use cases in which one TVM could requests secrets of another TVM when these TVMs exchange (or steal) tokens?
> 

I expect a proper key broker service to encrypt a released secret with a TVM ephemeral public key, included in the attestation token. An attestation token can only be used by a TVM owning the corresponding private key to unwrap the delivered secret. And it could be used to get secrets from a TSM, RoT or another TVM as long as you could establish an authenticated link with that entity.

> > For that purpose, I think we should first describe the generic local attestation flow for CoVE, that would look pretty similar to the remote attestation one. The attester requests an attestation evidence from the TSM but instead of sending it to a remote third party, submits it to e.g. another TVM through an implementation specific, trusted interface (e.g. following the [trustee attestation protocol](https://github.com/confidential-containers/trustee/blob/main/kbs/docs/kbs_attestation_protocol.md)). Following this we can describe how a CoVE TSM could, as a specific implementation of thee generic local attestation architecture, be used as either a verifier, a secret broker or both, and I think we want to differentiate those two services. This could be a sub section of the generic local attestation one:
> 
> I see the flow for releasing a token and using a token to retrieve secrets. What I am missing is how a TVM, which acts as a local secret broker, provisions the secrets in scenarios where only local attestation (no network) is available? It needs some component in the TCB, like the TSM or maybe RoT, to provide it with at least a key to decrypt other TVMs' TAPs. If this job is done by a TSM then we end up with the currently proposed model. If a TVM has access to a RoT, then this TVM becomes somehow special, more privileged "architectural" TVM. We would need to ensure at the architecture level that only this TVM can access the key in RoT.
> 

I agree, but I think that those two should be defined separately. An architectural TVM (similar to TDX's local attestation with the SGX enclave) is a valid use case but we first want to have a generic local attestation framework to support many models, including the one you're proposing in that PR but also e.g. the architectural TVM one.

> Other question is how other TVMs will retrieve the secrets? If the communicate with a TSM via `sbi_covt_get_secret()` then a TSM must somehow access the secret inside a local secret broker, right? Or would `sbi_covt_get_secret()` be somehow routed TVM->TSM->OS/VMM->TSM->LocalSecretBroker->TSM->OS/VMM->TSM->TVM?

The `sbi_covt_get_secret()` SBI would be to get a secret from the TSM. But in a TVM to TVM case, I don't think that the authenticated link between the two has to be architecturally defined, and I guess it does not have to go through the TSM. It could be any DH based protocol between the two (e.g. HTTPS), provided local connectivity is available. This would allow the secret broker to be in any security domain, including the host VMM one. > 
> Regarding the measurement section, yes, a crypto hash will hide the contents of the TVM image. Except for the fact that anyone seeing TAP understands whom it belongs to and what measurements will be verified, I agree that this section could be public, i.e., no confidentiality but only integrity protected. Maybe @gdhh has some more thoughts?

As long as the TAP has integrity protection it prevents someone from modifying. However, integrity protection alone does not prevent all attacks from all actors. Confidentiality and integrity protection prevents more attacks. In order for the integrity protection to be stronger we would also have to be limiting the size of the object or assuring that the number of bits verified in always part of the calculation of the final value. As I mentioned above, perhaps we should have a system where the creator of the TVM determines what is public and what is confidential.

body:
I agree that we can split functionality into two components: a local verifier and a local secret broker. We can show an example implementation, i.e., deployment model 3, in which the TSM implements both roles, but leave it open for other use cases.

Importantly, we cannot forget that the proposed `local attestation` mechanism offers not only secret delivery but also `authorization of a TVM execution`. (Otherwise, local attestation would be a variant of remote attestation with components executing in the same system, for some definition of system, as Guerney mentioned.) When creating a TVM, the TSM can use TAP to confirm that a TVM is authorized to run on the platform. If the TSM does not act as a secret broker, then TAP does not need to include any secrets, since they are not needed for authorization. However, a TAP containing secrets will always be required for a secret broker, though. So, right now, we have a TAP format that supports both.

Separating these roles offers greater design flexibility, but introduces additional complexity: (1) more ABI/API, (2) need to sync a secret broker's TAPs with a TVM's lifecycle.
